transcript.content: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?

I'm visiting today because I've been struggling with a severe lack of interest, low motivation, and feeling down for over a year. Along with that, I've been experiencing intense fluctuations in my mood and energy, sometimes feeling extremely elevated and irritable. It has just become too difficult to handle on my own.
When you have those elevated or irritable periods, do they last at least 4 days or even a week, and during them do you need much less sleep or do risky or unusual things?

Yes, those high-energy periods actually last much longer than a week—they've been going on for about five months now. During these times, I sleep significantly less but feel completely refreshed and don't feel the need for it. I don't really do dangerous things, but I become extremely hyperactive, talkative, and constantly switch between tasks.

During those five months, did these symptoms cause major problems like being unable to work or needing hospitalization, or did you ever have hallucinations or strongly fixed beliefs that others said were not true?

No, I never experienced any hallucinations or strongly fixed beliefs, and I didn't need to be hospitalized. Even though it was intense, I was still able to manage my daily life and keep working during those five months.
Over the past two years, have you felt depressed most days more often than not, with symptoms never going away for more than two months at a time?
No, I don't think it has been a full two years. But I have been struggling with these depressive feelings consistently for a bit over a year now, about a year and a month.

During those five months of elevated mood, did your symptoms clearly cause a marked change from your usual self that others noticed or that significantly strained your relationships, even if you kept working?

Yes, there was definitely a highly noticeable change, and people around me absolutely pointed out that I was acting differently. They were overwhelmed because I was talking incredibly fast, constantly switching tasks, and barely sleeping without ever feeling tired. My relationships were also strained because my mood would swing so rapidly from being extremely euphoric to suddenly very irritable.

Even though you kept working, during that five-month period did your symptoms ever become so severe that you were unable to function safely or appropriately in important situations, like at work, socially, or financially?

No, it never got to the point where I couldn't function safely or handle my responsibilities. I was extremely hyperactive and definitely difficult for others to be around, but I still managed to keep things under control at work and in my daily life.

Have you also had a separate period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day, with symptoms like loss of interest, low energy, sleep or appetite changes, guilt, or trouble concentrating?

Yes, I had a separate period of depression that lasted for about a year and a month. During that time, I completely lost interest in my hobbies, withdrew from friends, and had absolutely no motivation. I also had terrible sleep issues, where I'd struggle to fall asleep, wake up too early, or sometimes sleep too much but still feel completely unrefreshed.
During that five-month elevated period, did your symptoms ever clearly require hospitalization, include psychosis, or cause marked impairment so severe that you could not keep up normal functioning?

No, I never needed to be hospitalized, and I didn't experience any psychosis or lose touch with reality. Even though I was extremely energetic, talkative, and constantly active, I was still able to keep up my normal functioning and manage my daily life.

During those elevated periods, were these changes clearly different from your usual self and noticeable to others, but without ever becoming severe enough to cause hospitalization, psychosis, or inability to function?

Yes, absolutely. During those five months, my behavior—like barely sleeping, talking constantly, and starting multiple projects—was highly unusual for me and very noticeable to everyone around me. However, despite how intense it was, I never needed hospitalization, experienced any psychosis, or completely lost my ability to function.

The depressive episode is also well supported by over a year of low mood/anhedonia, withdrawal, low motivation, and sleep disturbance. Therefore the current candidate list narrows to Bipolar II Disorder.

Current candidates remain broad because the conversation has not yet clarified duration and severity of elevated states, presence of decreased need for sleep, impulsivity, psychosis, or functional impairment.
